## The Summation-of-Speed Story and Its Limits {#sec-lay-ch08}

## A Concrete Picture

Walk forward inside a train moving at $20$ m/s. If you walk at $2$ m/s relative
to the carriage, your ground velocity is $22$ m/s along the track. Walk backward
at the same speed and it is $18$ m/s. Velocities add as vectors; their magnitudes
add only when the vectors point in the same direction.

A clubhead likewise moves because its base moves and because the club changes
orientation. The geometry is less forgiving than a straight train aisle:
rotating segments continually change the directions of their contributions.
A large angular speed does not, by itself, tell us how much endpoint speed it
adds. Nor does an ordered series of speed peaks explain the forces that made
the movement possible.

![Schematic Peak Ordering With Overlapping Motion.](figures/proximal_distal_companion/fig_companion_sequence_overlap.svg){#fig-lay-sequence-overlap width=97% fig-alt="Four invented Gaussian angular-speed curves have separately normalized peaks in pelvis, trunk, hand, and club order. The curves illustrate timing and overlap only, not measured speed ratios, velocity contributions, or energy transfer."}

The figure uses chosen Gaussian curves, each scaled to its own peak. It shows
what an ordering could look like. It contains no human measurements, equations
of motion, calculated coupling, or contribution analysis. Equal normalized
heights do not mean equal segment speeds.

## How the Mechanism Works

### A Velocity Identity With Explicit Assumptions

Choose two material points on a rigid club: a grip point $H$ and a head point
$C$. Express their velocities and the club's angular velocity in the same
inertial frame. With $\mathbf r_{C/H}=\mathbf x_C-\mathbf x_H$,

$$
\mathbf v_C=\mathbf v_H+\boldsymbol\omega_{club}\times\mathbf r_{C/H}.
$$

Here $\boldsymbol\omega_{club}$ is the club's **absolute angular velocity**,
not its angular velocity relative to the forearm. The grip point can be
identified with a hand point only under a compatible no-slip contact assumption.
The identity holds in three dimensions; it does not require planar motion.

For a deforming shaft, write $\mathbf r_{C/H}=R(t)\boldsymbol\rho(t)$ where $R(t)$ rotates coordinates from a chosen moving club frame into the
inertial frame and $\boldsymbol\rho(t)$ is the displacement in that moving
frame. Differentiation adds $R\dot{\boldsymbol\rho}$ to the
transport and chosen-frame rotation terms. A slipping hand point also needs its relative
motion accounted for. A single rigid-body formula cannot silently include
shaft deformation or changing grip contact.

The rotational term has magnitude $\|\boldsymbol\omega\|r_\perp$, where
$r_\perp$ is the perpendicular distance from the angular-velocity axis through
$H$ to $C$. The familiar $v=r\omega$ uses that radius, not an arbitrary segment
length. A long club can amplify endpoint motion for a given angular rate;
kinematics alone says nothing about the torque, energy, or controllability
required to achieve it.

### A Two-Link Calculation That Exposes a Common Error

Take two links, each one metre long, in a plane with a fixed base. Let $q_1$ be the arm's
absolute angle and $q_2$ the club's angle relative to the arm, both positive
counterclockwise. The head position is

$$
\mathbf x_C=
\begin{bmatrix}
\cos q_1+\cos(q_1+q_2)\\
\sin q_1+\sin(q_1+q_2)
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

At $q_1=0$, $q_2=\pi/2$, $\dot q_1=2$ rad/s and $\dot q_2=3$ rad/s,
the hand velocity is $(0,2)$ m/s. The club's absolute angular rate is
$2+3=5$ rad/s, giving a rotational velocity $(-5,0)$ m/s and a total
$\mathbf v_C=(-5,2)$ m/s. Substituting the relative rate of $3$ rad/s into
the rigid-body formula would incorrectly give $(-3,2)$ m/s. It loses the
rotation of the club carried by the arm.

Differentiating the head position, or checking a small central time difference,
recovers $(-5,2)$. This is a geometric check on the convention, not a simulation
of a golfer or a demonstration of energy transfer.

### Joint Contributions Are a Declared Decomposition

For endpoint position $\mathbf x_C(\mathbf q)$, the Jacobian gives
$\mathbf v_C=J(\mathbf q)\dot{\mathbf q}$. Include moving-base coordinates
among $\mathbf q$, or add their transport explicitly. If position depends
explicitly on time, its partial time derivative is another term. Generalized
speeds that differ from $\dot{\mathbf q}$ require the corresponding mapping.

In the two-link example the Jacobian columns at that posture are $(-1,1)$ and
$(-1,0)$. Their rate-weighted contributions are $(-2,2)$ and $(-3,0)$ m/s.
These sum to the same head velocity as the hand-plus-club decomposition, but
allocate it differently. The first joint rotates both links; hand translation
alone is not its entire Jacobian contribution.

For any declared vector decomposition $\mathbf v_C=\sum_i\mathbf v_i$ with
nonzero total velocity, a useful signed speed partition is

$$
c_i=\frac{\mathbf v_C}{\|\mathbf v_C\|}\mathbin{\cdot}\mathbf v_i,
\qquad \sum_i c_i=\|\mathbf v_C\|.
$$

These projections can be negative. Keep the posture and arm rate above, but
set $\dot q_2=-5$ rad/s. The contributions become $(-2,2)$ and $(5,0)$ m/s;
total velocity is $(3,2)$ m/s. Their projections are $-2/\sqrt{13}$ and
$15/\sqrt{13}$ m/s, summing to $\sqrt{13}$ m/s. Large component magnitudes
would overestimate the actual speed if simply added.

The partition depends on the selected point, coordinates, reference motion and
choice of terms. A common orthogonal rotation of the axes leaves these dot
products unchanged; changing the decomposition is a different operation.
At zero endpoint speed the unit direction, and therefore this partition, is
undefined.

A negative projection does **not** establish negative joint power. Even the
translational kinetic energy of a point mass contains cross terms:

$$
\frac12 m\left\|\sum_i\mathbf v_i\right\|^2
=\frac12 m\sum_i\|\mathbf v_i\|^2
+m\sum_{i<j}\mathbf v_i\mathbin{\cdot}\mathbf v_j.
$$

For the opposing example with $m=1$ kg, total energy is $6.5$ J, whereas
adding the two separate squared-speed energies gives $16.5$ J. The cross term
is $-10$ J. A whole golfer also has distributed mass and rotational energy.
Speed projections are neither segment energy shares nor causal allocations
of the work that created the state.

### Peak Time Is Not Transfer Time

A smooth signed scalar velocity component has zero derivative at an interior
extremum. For nonzero three-dimensional angular velocity, however,

$$
\frac{d\|\boldsymbol\omega\|}{dt}
=\frac{\boldsymbol\omega\mathbin{\cdot}\boldsymbol\alpha}
       {\|\boldsymbol\omega\|},
\qquad \boldsymbol\alpha=\frac{d\boldsymbol\omega}{dt}.
$$

A smooth interior angular-speed peak requires
$\boldsymbol\omega\cdot\boldsymbol\alpha=0$, not
$\boldsymbol\alpha=\mathbf0$. For a dimensionless manufactured example near
$t=0$, take $\boldsymbol\omega(t)=(1-t^2)(\cos t,\sin t,0)$.
Its magnitude reaches $1$ at $t=0$ while $\boldsymbol\alpha(0)=(0,1,0)$:
the rotation axis is changing direction. A stationary derivative alone does
not prove a maximum; endpoints, plateaus, noise and nonsmooth signals need
separate event rules.

Report whether a peak belongs to an absolute segment angular-speed norm, a
relative joint rate, or an anatomical component. Merely re-expressing the same
physical vector in orthonormal axes cannot change its norm or its peak time.
Switching from an absolute rate to a relative joint rate, or selecting a
component, can change the reported peak time. Filtering,
differentiation, time normalization and event detection can also alter the
reported ordering; near ties need uncertainty intervals rather than a forced
ranking.

Power answers a different question. For applied force $\mathbf F$ and moment
$\mathbf M$ at a declared rigid-body contact point, $P=\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v+\mathbf M\cdot\boldsymbol\omega$, with moment
and velocity referred consistently to that point. For a rotational joint, net joint power uses the
joint moment and compatible relative angular velocity. Interface power,
net joint power, segment energy change and external work are related ledgers,
not interchangeable labels. Integrate the powers over a declared interval and compare the resulting work
with changes in stored energy to test the account. Angular-speed peak times
cannot close it.

### What the Human and Model Evidence Establishes

**Human Evidence:** Tinmark and colleagues studied 45 golfers: 11 male tournament
professionals, 21 male elite amateurs and 13 female elite amateurs. They recorded
pelvis, upper-torso and hand motion at 240 Hz and calculated resultant angular-speed
magnitudes. Their reported ordering and increasing peaks occurred across the
partial and full-shot conditions studied [@tinmark2010]. This is evidence about
those measured segments and definitions. It does not supply a club-energy ledger,
prove that every individual trial follows one order, or experimentally identify
an optimal torque schedule. The authors' interpretation involving interaction
torques goes beyond the directly reported kinematic observations.

**Mechanistic Evidence From Other Tasks:** Putnam's 1991 analysis used four
subjects performing kicking, walking and running, and examined thigh--leg
interaction terms [@putnam1991]. It supports investigating motion-dependent
interaction, not transferring a lower-limb result unqualified to golf. The later
striking-and-throwing review synthesizes descriptions and explanations
[@putnam1993]. Milburn's golf paper presents a double-pendulum analysis of the
downswing [@milburn1982]; its model conclusions should be stated with their
assumptions rather than counted as independent proof of a universal human rule.

**Model Result:** The pinned uncertainty study uses a planar moving-base,
two-hand, flexible-club model with bounded surrogate actuators. Delivery is
evaluated at a fixed $0.24$ s, without a ball collision; its speeds are not
calibrated full-swing human performance. All eight preselected control programs
are nondominated across five objectives on six synthetic held-out cases: lower-tail
delivery speed, planar face/path error, upper-tail hand force, squared-torque
effort proxy, and speed dispersion. That means no other member of this finite comparison
set is at least as good in every objective and strictly better in one. It does
not imply every possible improvement incurs a cost, or that these programs form
the continuous optimum over all controls.

Speed alone selects `early_restrain`: its tenth-percentile delivery speed is
highest among these candidates, about $4.706$ m/s. This ranking does not settle
a choice across all five objectives. The saved comparisons do not analyze
segment-peak sequences, validate human strategies, or establish that different
human sequences achieve the same result.

**Hypothesis:** A useful strategy may arrange geometry and motion so that the
club's rotational contribution aligns favorably with grip-point velocity near
the chosen impact event, while satisfying face, path, load and robustness
requirements. Whether that strategy improves performance requires trajectory
and intervention evidence. Instantaneous vector alignment is not an optimization
result or a prescription for when a golfer should release the club.

### A Sequence as a Testable Constraint

A proximal peak can precede a distal peak because proximal drive changes,
because interaction loads change, or because the measured vector changes
magnitude or direction. Several mechanisms can coexist. Proximal slowing also
need not mean that every associated joint has negative power. The links remain
coupled while their speeds rise and fall; a peak does not disconnect one segment
and hand its motion to the next.

Build the explanation around synchronized observations: segment and joint
kinematics, external and grip wrenches, declared interface powers, segment
energies, and uncertainty. Define transition and impact events explicitly.
Then ask whether a proposed mechanism predicts the force direction, moment
sign and energy changes as well as the peak order. A model with the right order
but the wrong power history has not explained that history.

If the arm-dominant and wrist-dominant proposals reproduce similar motion,
bilateral wrenches and motion can constrain their external mechanical
allocations. Activation measurements can add physiological evidence, but they
do not uniquely identify muscle forces or neural commands. More measurements
are useful only insofar as they discriminate the competing predictions; see
@sec-lay-ch21 for identifiability.

### Reader Lab: Separate Motion From Its Causes

Reproduce the two-link velocity with a central finite difference of position.
Plot its Jacobian contributions tip-to-tail, then use the opposing-rate example
to calculate signed projections and the energy cross term. Change posture while
holding rates fixed. The arrows change because geometry participates in the
mapping, even before a dynamics model has been introduced.

Next, plot the manufactured angular-velocity vector above and its norm. At the
norm peak, check both the acceleration vector and its dot product with velocity.
This prevents the zero-acceleration interpretation from entering a subsequent
sequence analysis. With measured data, repeat peak detection across justified
filter settings and report ambiguous orderings instead of selecting a preferred
plot.

Finally, in a forward dynamics model, copy a state and remove a finite proximal
torque while retaining positions, velocities and the same constraints. The
instantaneous endpoint velocity is unchanged. Acceleration can change through
the constrained equations of motion, and the subsequent trajectories can diverge;
it is not guaranteed that every endpoint acceleration component changes.
Impulses, contact changes and prescribed-motion constraints require separate
handling. An existing velocity contribution is distinct from continuing actuator
power, and a finite-time response is distinct from the copied-state comparison.

### Responsible Practical Translation

A sequence plot can locate a phase worth investigating and test whether a model
reproduces a measured coordination feature. It becomes more informative when
paired with within-person repeatability and predicted responses to perturbation.
A reliably successful counterexample would refute a claim that one exact ordering
is necessary under those conditions. Observing the order alone would not establish
sufficiency or reveal its cause.

For coaching or equipment analysis, evaluate the whole declared objective and
the uncertainty of the change. Do not turn population peak times into commands
to stop one segment before starting another. State-based timing, such as an event
near a particular arm--club configuration, is a candidate for testing across
tempos rather than an established replacement rule.

## Where the Picture Breaks

The train analogy explains instantaneous velocity addition. It leaves out the
reaction forces, changing geometry, elastic motion and control that determine
a swing trajectory. Increasing every segment's angular speed does not guarantee
a faster, better-directed clubhead at the event of interest.

The chapter's central distinction is between three questions: how current motions
combine, when a selected speed reaches its peak, and how forces and work created
or changed the state. Jacobians answer the first, defined events answer the
second, and dynamics with explicit power boundaries addresses the third. A strong
swing explanation connects all three without using one as a substitute for another.
